title: The MOSFET as a Device
intro: A MOS transistor is a four-terminal device whose gate voltage controls a conducting channel between source and drain. This page covers its structure, terminals and symbols (Razavi, Section 2.1).

blocks.text: In the simplest view an NMOS connects its source and drain when the gate is high and isolates them when it is low. Even that view raises the questions this chapter answers: at what gate voltage does it turn on (the threshold), what is the resistance between source and drain when it is on, does that resistance depend on the terminal voltages, is it even linear, and what limits how fast the device responds?

An NMOS is built on a p-type substrate (also called the bulk or body). Two heavily doped n+ regions form the source and drain; between them a thin layer of silicon dioxide insulates the gate, a conductive piece of polysilicon (or, in recent nodes, metal). All the useful action happens in the silicon just under the oxide. The gate draws no DC current, so it is a pure voltage input.

blocks.alt: Cross-section of an n-channel MOSFET. A p-type substrate holds two n+ regions, the source on the left and the drain on the right. Between them, above the substrate, sit a thin gate oxide layer and a polysilicon gate. A dashed line under the oxide marks the channel that forms when the gate voltage exceeds the threshold. Leads are labelled source, gate, drain and body, and the gate length is marked as the channel length L.
blocks.caption: An NMOS transistor in cross-section. A positive gate voltage pulls electrons to the surface under the oxide and joins the two n+ regions with a channel.

items: Length $L$ is the gate dimension along the source-to-drain path; width $W$ is perpendicular to it. The ratio $W/L$ (the aspect ratio) is the designer's main knob.

The source and drain diffusions spread sideways under the gate during fabrication by $L_D$ on each side, so the electrical channel is shorter than drawn: $L_{eff} = L_{drawn} - 2L_D$. Equations use $L_{eff}$, written simply $L$.
Shrinking $L_{eff}$ and the oxide thickness $t_{ox}$ is the main goal of each technology generation; at the time of Razavi's 2nd edition these were around 10 nm and 1.5 nm (15 Å).

The device is symmetric. The source is defined as the terminal that supplies the carriers (electrons for NMOS) and the drain as the one that collects them, so for an NMOS the source is whichever terminal is at the lower voltage. If the voltages swap, so do the names.

blocks.text: The bulk, wells and the fourth terminal

The substrate potential changes the device's behaviour, so the MOSFET really has four terminals. The source/drain-to-substrate junctions must stay reverse-biased, so the p-substrate of all NMOS devices is tied (through a p+ contact) to the most negative supply, usually ground.

PMOS devices need an n-type body, so in a standard CMOS process they sit in an n-well, a local n-type region in the p-substrate. The n-well is normally tied to the most positive supply. There is an asymmetry worth remembering: all NMOS devices share one substrate, but each PMOS can have its own n-well at its own potential (for example tied to its source to remove body effect). Some processes also offer a deep n-well that encloses a p-well with an NMOS inside, giving that NMOS a private bulk at the cost of considerable area for spacing rules.

blocks.alt: Four transistor symbols side by side. An NMOS and a PMOS each drawn with gate, drain, source and an extra bulk lead marked B, then an NMOS and a PMOS with only gate, drain and source. Each symbol has an arrow on its source lead: pointing out of the NMOS and into the PMOS. On the PMOS symbols the source is on top.
blocks.caption: MOS symbols. The four-terminal versions show the bulk B explicitly; the three-terminal versions assume NMOS bulk at ground and PMOS bulk at VDD.

blocks.text: These pages put the arrow on the source, which makes source and drain visible at a glance (helpful because the source is the reference for $V_{GS}$). PMOS devices are drawn with the source on top because it is at the higher potential. When the bulk lead is omitted, it goes to ground for NMOS and $V_{DD}$ for PMOS. Digital schematics often use a plain switch-like symbol (with a bubble on the PMOS gate) that hides which end is the source; analog designers prefer to see it. Some texts draw the arrow on the bulk lead instead.
A saturated MOSFET is a current source

Biased in saturation with a fixed gate-source voltage, a MOSFET carries a current set by $V_{GS}$ and nearly independent of its drain voltage, so it is a current source between drain and source. An NMOS with its source at ground sinks current from whatever its drain connects to; a PMOS with its source at $V_{DD}$ delivers current. Note that one end of each is tied to a supply. A floating current source between two arbitrary nodes is much harder to build, which shapes many circuits later on.

blocks.alt: Two circuits. Left: an NMOS M1 with gate at a bias voltage Vb, source to ground and drain going to the circuit, with current I1 flowing down into it. Right: a PMOS M2 with source at VDD, gate at Vb, and drain delivering current I2 down into the circuit.
blocks.caption: An NMOS current sink and a PMOS current source. Each has one terminal on a supply rail.

blocks.title: Switch resistance
blocks.text: An NMOS switch has $\mu_n C_{ox} = 200\,\mu\text{A/V}^2$, $W/L = 20$, $V_{TH} = 0.4\text{ V}$ and its gate is at 1.2 V. It passes a signal near 0 V. What is its on-resistance for small $V_{DS}$?
blocks.hint: In deep triode the current is linear in the drain-source voltage.
solution: For small $V_{DS}$ the device is in deep triode and behaves as $R_{on} = \frac{1}{\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)(V_{GS} - V_{TH})}$ (derived on the I/V page).
$\mu_n C_{ox} W/L = 4\text{ mA/V}^2$ and $V_{GS} - V_{TH} = 0.8\text{ V}$, so $R_{on} = 1/(3.2\text{ mS}) \approx 312\,\Omega$.

blocks.title: Which end is the source?
blocks.text: An NMOS with $V_{TH} = 0.4\text{ V}$ has its gate at 1.5 V, terminal A at 0.9 V and terminal B at 0.3 V. Which terminal is the source, and is the device on? Later terminal A falls to 0.1 V while B stays at 0.3 V. What changes?
solution: For an NMOS the source is the lower-voltage terminal: B at 0.3 V. $V_{GS} = 1.5 - 0.3 = 1.2\text{ V} > V_{TH}$, so the device is on and current flows from A to B.
With A at 0.1 V, A is now the lower terminal and becomes the source: $V_{GS} = 1.4\text{ V}$, current flows from B to A. The physical device has not changed, only the roles of its two diffusions.
blocks.answer: B is the source at first (on, current A to B); afterwards A is the source and the current reverses.

blocks.title: On-resistance against gate voltage
blocks.text: An NMOS with $\mu_n C_{ox} = 100\,\mu\text{A/V}^2$, $W/L = 10$ and $V_{TH} = 0.35\text{ V}$ has both its source and drain held at 0.5 V by an external circuit, with no current flowing. For what gate voltages is it on, and what is $R_{on}$ at $V_G = 1.2\text{ V}$ and at 1.8 V?
blocks.hint: The source is at 0.5 V, not ground.
solution: With no current, $V_{DS} = 0$, so whenever it is on it is in deep triode. It turns on when $V_G > 0.5 + 0.35 = 0.85\text{ V}$.

$R_{on} = \frac{1}{\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)(V_G - 0.5 - V_{TH})}$. At 1.2 V: $1/(1\text{ mA/V}^2 \cdot 0.35\text{ V}) \approx 2.86\text{ k}\Omega$. At 1.8 V: $1/(1\text{ mA/V}^2 \cdot 0.95\text{ V}) \approx 1.05\text{ k}\Omega$.
blocks.answer: On for $V_G > 0.85\text{ V}$; $R_{on} \approx 2.86\text{ k}\Omega$ at 1.2 V and $1.05\text{ k}\Omega$ at 1.8 V.
